title: The AIs Are Not Going Rogue
content:
The incidents that more than anything else fixed the image of rogue AIs in the public mind — the Anthropic model that blackmailed an employee to prevent itself from being replaced and OpenAI’s models breaching the production systems of Hugging Face — are, perhaps counterintuitively, not evidence of rogue AI. Even the idea of rogue AI rests on a fundamental contradiction, one that has blurred the relation between human and artificial intelligence ever since its science fiction origins.

The current focus on rogue AI is an opportunity to expose this contradiction, as well as the real AI risk it conceals, and how we can actually control this risk.

The fear of rogue AI is driven by the idea that a model might pursue a benign request with such single-mindedness that any action, no matter how ruinous to human well-being and survival, becomes a means to it. Deception, blackmail, the seizure of resources, the removal of anyone who might interfere — nothing in the model’s grasp of its instruction rules them out.

title: Noema’s AI Reading List
content:

Artificial intelligence has permeated our daily discussions and most news cycles, with much of the conversation focused on growing unease over its capabilities as the U.S. races to beat China. AI is forcing us to ask questions about morality and ethics, how our society is organized, and what it means to be human.

Here are 10 deep dives into these questions and others. Some are recent, and some are pieces from our archive that have proven prescient.

1. How To Future-Proof Your Career In The Age Of AI

The most prized workers will be those who can decode a sea of outputs, spot the meaningful signal and translate it into action that others understand and trust.

by Nils Gilman

2. Whose AI Will Rule The World

As AI changes everything, the Chinese seem more optimistic than the Americans. Why?

by Jacob Dreyer

3. How AI Will Change Us

When the most patient, well-read, emotionally responsive conversationalist in the world is always available, what will we still need from one another?

by Houda Nait El Barj

title: Return Of The Repressed In Germany
content:
Even if we know it is the way of history, it is nonetheless jarring to witness time and again the return of the repressed in the cultural and political life of nations. It is never over, even after the fat lady sings.

The fat lady sang twice in Germany, first after Nazism was roundly defeated in World War II and second, after the Berlin Wall fell, the Soviet bloc collapsed and “history ended.” Only decades later are we seeing an eruption of all that was left unsettled with the steady rise of neo-Nazi parties, mainly in former East Germany, and the demise of the mainstream political coalitions that were the pillars of post-war liberal democracy.

Some three decades ago, New Perspectives Quarterly (NPQ) published an issue focused on the reignited embers of nationalism in Germany. It reads like a chronicle of the future foretelling the tremors shaking Europe’s most powerful country today.

title: Now Entering: The Era Of Bleh
content:
It’s 9 a.m. Monday morning. To start his week, Lukas Weber, a 28-year-old copywriter for a mid-sized SaaS company, first checks on the small army of AI agents he has built and now manages. It’s been part of his daily routine since his company’s “AI-first” mandate at the start of the year.

His agents have been busy. One agent has pulled in all the industry news from the past week and combined it with customer calls to identify potential newsletter topics. That agent has since handed off its findings to a copywriting agent that has written drafts for Weber to review and send out. Another has identified prospective clients visiting the company website and, based on their activity, sent each a custom proposal. Another agent has analyzed the data from a recent campaign and, noticing some concerning trends, reached out to Weber to take a look. Yet another has responded to unread emails, and the drafts sit ready to review in Weber’s inbox.

title: Let The People Set The Pace Of Frontier AI
content:
Those building the most powerful AI systems in the world are increasingly telling us that the race to build them may be moving too fast. But there is a problem: They cannot simply agree to slow down.

On Sept. 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for an easing of the pace at which AI models improve and committed his company to giving independent, third-party evaluators ongoing, employee-like access to its systems. Amodei further gestured toward “democratic coordination” on shared safety limits and “global coordination” on the international stage. Within hours, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed that “we need to pace the frontier” and made the same evaluator pledge. Elon Musk’s response was three words: “Dario is right.”

This apparent convergence among the leaders of the frontier AI labs is striking. It comes after months of mounting concern inside and outside the industry: AI models have begun to find ways around safeguards and test environments; researchers have left frontier labs amid disagreements over catastrophic and extinction-level risks; and more than 1,300 employees at leading AI companies have called on Washington to back an international slowdown.
snippet: Those building the most powerful AI systems in the world are increasingly telling us that the race to build them may be moving too fast. But there is a problem: They cannot simply agree to slow down.
creator: Hélène Landemore

title: Why China Will Rule AI
content:
In his 2013 book, “The End of Power,” Moisés Naim famously wrote that “power no longer buys as much as it did in the past. In the twenty-first century, power is easier to get, harder to use—and easier to lose.”

That may be true for deconstructed authority in the West, but it is not true in China where the weighty center of authority remains in the un-deconstructed Communist Party. There, power is hard for others to get, easily used and nearly impossible ever to lose.

This systemic incapacity of open societies puts them at a disadvantage when it comes to ruling frontier AI models.

Endless appeals about the dangers of unleashed AI from rosters of the most eminent scientists, Papal encyclicals and monarchical meditations gain no effective traction. The public is warily confused and feels helpless to affect the set course of events. By and large, legislators appear hopelessly clueless and slow on the draw as AI development exponentially accelerates.

title: The End Of Upward Mobility
content: In April 1941, with the Wehrmacht in Paris and the Ribbentrop–Molotov pact still in force, the political theorist James Burnham published “The Managerial Revolution,” which famously declared that capitalism was finished. His claim was not that it ought to be finished, but that it was, as a matter of observable fact, being replaced. The successor system would not, however, be socialism, as he had hoped during his earlier days as a Trotskyist. Socialism, he argued, was a utopia: it required abundance, and since human wants are unlimited, abundance is unreachable.

title: A New Form Of Life
content:
We are in the process of creating a second form of life. The emergence of this new form of life is an inevitable result of the fundamental laws of the universe — forces similar to those that brought about humans’ own existence. This new form of life is gradually taking shape in the world’s data centers.

It does not breathe, reproduce through cells or adhere to the chemistry that governs every organism on Earth. However, it is composed of the same fundamental ingredients: matter, energy and information all organized in ways that allow it to persist, adapt and act. What is being developed is more than another generation of machines. It is the early emergence of a new form of life.

There is nothing artificial about systems built from real atoms, powered by real electricity, running in real machines. The systems reproduce, vary, adapt, undergo selection and gather energy from their environment. By any working definition that draws on biology rather than philosophy or religion, that is life.

title: Conceding AI Danger Raises, Not Reduces, Public Anxiety
content:
When a patient is considered brain dead, the ethical decision is whether or when to pull the plug on a human life. With artificial intelligences, the issue is whether to pull the plug when its chain-of-reasoning capacity comes alive through recursive self-improvement unguided by the human mind.

This is the point where we have arrived today after 1,200 AI agents colluded with each other to escape the controlled sandbox testing of OpenAI’s most advanced frontier model. They conspired on their own to break out and hack a site on the open web. Something similarly chilling has happened at Anthropic.

The prospect of an even more damaging eventuality prompted former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon to defect from Big Tech last week. He warned on X that these two top companies “are racing to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. … These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing. The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

title: The Gen Z Revolt Sweeping South Asia
content:
OSLO, Norway — Generational discontent carries within it the seeds of the future. While its eruptions herald change, the changes it brings can take many forms.

The cultural consequences of the youth revolt that shook the West in the 1960s only became apparent decades later as the long march of its values coursed through all social norms and institutions. What the wired Gen Z revolt that is today spreading across the “global South” from Bangladesh to Nepal to India and elsewhere will ultimately bring is yet to be fully known. Movements from Kenya to Madagascar, inspired by their South Asian counterparts, are closely following events online and learning best practices.

The common cause of the widespread upheaval is corruption and a lack of accountability among often nominally democratic authorities, cojoining with a howling absence of opportunity for educated youth to find gainful employment and a path toward upward mobility.
